problem: Prior open-vocabulary semantic map methods for VLN (VLMaps, NLMap-SayCan) are instance-agnostic, so they cannot resolve instance-specific commands such as 'the fourth chair' or 'the second counter'. They are also memory-heavy because they store high-dimensional LSeg embeddings per cell.
motivation: Realistic commands refer to individual instances through spatial or viewpoint relations, and the referred object may not be in the current view. A global top-down map with instance identities allows ranking and relating instances for planning. Dropping feature embeddings could also make the map far cheaper and less noisy.
key_idea: Build an embedding-free top-down grid map labeled with panoptic-segmentation object classes, then split each class's cells into instances with Louvain community detection on a graph whose edge weights come from same-instance co-occurrence in per-frame masks.
insight: Per-frame instance masks, aggregated across frames with community detection, recover instances even when objects are adjacent, where connected components merge them. The table shows the gain: SI Maps reach 0.80 human-evaluated SR versus 0.34 for VLMaps with connected components and 0.24 for plain VLMaps. Qualitatively, SI Maps recover 32 chair-type segments against 29 real ones, while connected components merge dining chairs. Constraining the map with segmentation masks instead of embedding-text alignment also gives a cleaner map.
method: Occupancy grid with semantic labels: back-project RGB-D pixels with pose into a 0.05 m top-down grid M (H×W×2) storing <object class, instance id>. Class labels come from Mask2Former (COCO panoptic), and the highest point wins when several pixels fall in one cell.

Instance graph: for each object class, cells form nodes. The edge weight between the cells of two neighbouring pixels increases by 1 whenever they share the same panoptic instance in a frame. Weights are normalized by how many times the cells were observed.

Louvain community detection: iterates modularity optimization and community aggregation to group cells into instances. It suppresses spurious edges caused by imperfect masks, unlike connected components.
Post-processing merge: communities C1 and C2 are merged if more than K% of C1's members neighbor some member of C2, correcting over-segmentation. K is tunable (5 or 9 tested).

LLM-based language navigation: ChatGPT is given 23 function primitives and few-shot examples, plus the list of objects in the map. It generates Python code whose primitive calls carry an instance parameter (e.g. nth closest object, between two objects). A* on the map executes the plan.
Memory efficiency: no LSeg embeddings are stored, so a 1000×1000 map takes about 16 MB versus about 2 GB for VLMaps.

setting.backbone: Mask2Former (COCO panoptic, pretrained) + ChatGPT (frozen, few-shot) + Louvain clustering
setting.training_data: none (training-free; pretrained Mask2Former on COCO, ChatGPT few-shot prompts)
setting.observation: RGB-D frames with camera pose (5,267 frames from 5 Matterport3D scenes)
setting.action_space: Function primitives (23) executed via A* path planning on the top-down map in continuous space
setting.privileged: Ground-truth poses for map building; automatic evaluation uses the ground-truth environment map

numbers.eval_set_note: Custom instance-specific language queries on 5 Matterport3D scenes; the number of queries is not stated

numbers_note: Success rates are printed as fractions (0.80), not percentages, and are kept as printed. The test queries are custom rather than an official benchmark, and their count is not given. Baselines: VLMaps 0.24 human / 0.46 auto; VLMaps with CC 0.34 / 0.48.
results: SI Maps (K=5) reach 0.80 human-evaluated and 0.88 automatic SR, against 0.24/0.46 for VLMaps and 0.34/0.48 for VLMaps with connected components (the strongest baseline). This is the 233% improvement claimed in the abstract. The map is also about 128× smaller (16 MB vs 2 GB).
limitations: Restricted to COCO closed-set classes from Mask2Former, so it is not truly open-vocabulary. The abstract's claim of open-set association via LLM word ontology is barely developed in the text.

Small custom evaluation (5 scenes, a query set of unstated size) in simulation only, with no standard benchmark. Relies on ground-truth poses and 2D per-frame instance masks, with residual noisy segments.
Requires hyperparameter K, and the LLM must generate correct code.
